intro: One tree, standing in the middle of a road junction. The Great Zelkova of Haramachi, one of Japan's three great zelkovas, is roughly 1,000 years old, hollow and steel-propped since the 1960s, with traffic on two prefectural roads still routed around it. In 1868 townspeople stopped an official from felling it for lumber when the saw revealed sap that looked like blood. A National Natural Monument since 1933, free, in the open, no ticket needed.
meta_description: The Great Zelkova of Haramachi, Gunma: one of Japan's three great zelkovas, roughly 1,000 years old, standing in a road junction. Free.
question_meta: Higashiagatsuma's mapped tree is the Great Zelkova of Haramachi, roughly 1,000 years old, one of Japan's three great zelkovas.
question_answer: Higashiagatsuma's mapped tree is the Great Zelkova of Haramachi, one of the trio Japan itself names its three great zelkovas (alongside Higashine's and the already-published Great Zelkova of Mitsue). Its age is put at roughly 1,000 years, and it has been in visible decline since about 1965: hollow, propped on steel pipes, kept alive mainly by roots grown inside its own cavity.
question_context: A 1932 survey by Miyoshi Manabu, who drew up the original list of Japan's three great zelkovas, measured this tree at 16.89 metres round at the roots and 10.97 at chest height, with one limb reaching 22 metres. A 2021 survey gives 9.10 metres at chest height, a real decline rather than a different convention: branches are gone, the trunk is largely a shell, and steel pipes now carry much of the crown. Its age, roughly 1,000 years, has never been narrowed further. The tree stands in the middle of a public road junction where two Gunma prefectural roads meet, and townspeople have twice acted to protect it: in 1868 an official proposed felling it for timber for the new prefectural government building, and the plan stopped the moment the saw revealed the trunk was already hollow, with sap that looked like blood. Local tradition holds the town's streets were laid out in 1614 along a sightline between this tree and a rock formation behind Iwabitsu Castle, and the old name for zelkova, Tsukinoki, became the neighbourhood's name. A cutting from the tree grows at the town sports ground as insurance.

faq.q: What is special about this tree?
faq.a: It is one of the Three Great Zelkovas of Japan (日本三大欅), a trio a 1932 survey named alongside the zelkovas of Higashine and Mitsue. It stands in the middle of a road junction, hollow and propped since the 1960s.
Roughly 1,000 years, a figure that has never been narrowed further by any source.
Yes, it stands in the open on a public road junction with nothing to book or ask permission for.
About 10 to 15 minutes on foot from JR Gumma-Haramachi Station on the Agatsuma Line.

trees.story:
One of Japan's three great zelkovas stands in the middle of a road junction. Traffic in Haramachi goes around it, where two Gunma prefectural roads meet. In 1868 an official proposed felling it for timber for the new prefectural government building. Townspeople objected, and when the saw went in it found the trunk already hollow, with sap that looked like blood. The work stopped there. Locals called it Tsukinoki, an old word for zelkova, long enough for the name to become the name of the place, and tradition holds that the town's streets were laid out in 1614 along a sightline between this trunk and a rock formation behind Iwabitsu Castle.

The botanist Miyoshi Manabu, whose 1932 survey drew up the trio, measured it then at 16.89 metres round at the roots and 10.97 at chest height, with one limb reaching 22 metres to the northeast. A 2021 prefectural survey gives 17 metres tall and 9.10 metres round. Much of that gap is loss. Vigour has fallen away since about 1965, branches are gone, the trunk is largely a shell, and what keeps it alive are roots that grew down inside its own cavity. Steel pipes carry the rest. Its age is put at roughly a thousand years and nobody has narrowed it further. A cutting from it grows at the town sports ground, as insurance.
trees.access: Free, no ticket, always visible. It stands literally in the middle of a public road junction (where Gunma Prefectural Roads 35 and 58 meet) in the middle of town, braced with steel pipe supports since its decline. Nothing to book, nothing to ask permission for.
trees.transport: About 10-15 minutes on foot from JR Gumma-Haramachi Station (Agatsuma Line)
